prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

There is a two-headed goat, a four-winged chicken and a sad lamb with seven legs whose complicated little life was spent in Hopland, California. I saw the man with doubled eyes who seemed to watch in me my doubts about my spirit. Will it snag upon this aging flesh? There is a strawberry that grew out of a carrot plant, a blade of grass that lanced through a thick rock, a cornstalk nineteen-feet-two-inches tall grown by George Osborne of Silome, Arkansas. There is something grotesque growing in me I cannot tell. It has been waxing, burgeoning, for a long time. It weighs me down like the chains of the man of Lahore who began collecting links on his naked body until he crawled around the town carrying the last thirteen years of his life six-hundred-seventy pounds. Each link or each lump in me is an offense against love. I want my own lit candle lamp buried in my skull like the Lighthouse Man of Chungking, who could lead the travelers home. Well, I am still a traveler and I don’t know where I live. If my home is here, inside my breast, light it up! And I will invite you in as my first guest.

outputs.L1:
There is a two-headed goat, a four-winged chicken, and a sad, seven-legged lamb whose complicated little life was spent in Hopland, California. I saw the man with doubled eyes, who seemed to see within me my doubts about my spirit: Will it snag upon this aging flesh?

There is a strawberry that grew from a carrot plant, a blade of grass that lanced through thick rock, and a cornstalk—nineteen feet, two inches tall—grown by George Osborne of Silome, Arkansas. There is something grotesque growing in me, though I cannot say what. It has been waxing, burgeoning, for a long time. Each link—or each lump within me—is an offense against love. I want a lighted candle-lamp buried in my skull, like the Lighthouse Man of Chungking, who could lead travelers home. outputs.L2: In Hopland, California, lived a goat with two heads, a chicken bearing four wings, and a melancholy seven-legged lamb whose brief existence was tangled with hardship. I encountered a man with two sets of eyes, and he appeared to see within me all my uncertainty about the fate of my spirit: will it catch on this body as it grows old? A strawberry once emerged from a carrot plant; a single blade of grass pierced a massive rock; and George Osborne of Silome, Arkansas, raised a cornstalk measuring nineteen feet two inches. Something misshapen is also taking root inside me, though I cannot name it. For years it has swelled and spread, burdening me like the chains worn by the man from Lahore, who kept adding links to his bare body until, after thirteen years, he could only creep through town beneath six hundred seventy pounds of them. Every link in his load—and every growth within me—is a violation of love. I long to have a burning lamp enclosed in my skull, as the Lighthouse Man of Chungking did, so that I might guide travelers home. Yet I remain a traveler myself, unsure where I belong. If my home lies here within my chest, then illuminate it, and I will welcome you as its very first guest.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by describing bizarre anomalies in the natural world, including animals born with multiple limbs and plants that have taken on strange, unnatural forms. Encounters with similarly unusual human figures lead the speaker toward a deeper question: what becomes of the spirit when it is confined within a body altered and weakened by age?

This reflection turns inward. The speaker senses a grotesque burden within—a presence that has grown steadily over time and now weighs heavily upon them. They compare it to a mass of accumulated chains, in which every inner “link” represents an offense against love: a failure to give it, receive it, or remain faithful to it.

Despite this oppressive weight, the speaker still longs for illumination, intimacy, and a sense of belonging. They hope to discover a true home within their own heart, a place made open and welcoming through self-understanding. From there, they wish to invite another person in, offering both of them the possibility of connection, acceptance, and shared refuge.
outputs.L4:
The speaker begins by surveying a world filled with grotesque natural anomalies and unsettling human oddities. Misshapen creatures, strange bodies, and distorted forms become more than curiosities: they reflect a universe in which the familiar has been made foreign. This catalog of abnormalities creates an atmosphere of estrangement, suggesting that disorder exists not only in nature and society but also within the speaker’s own consciousness.

Beneath these outward images lies an inward spiritual burden. The speaker feels marked by difference, unable to locate a secure place in the world or to understand where the soul truly belongs. The strange beings described throughout the catalog therefore serve as mirrors of an internal condition. Their physical irregularities embody the speaker’s emotional isolation, uncertainty, and fear of being separated from others. What appears at first to be an inventory of external wonders gradually becomes an exploration of loneliness and identity.

Yet the speaker does not remain trapped in alienation. The search for belonging turns inward, toward the heart as a possible home for the wandering soul. Rather than seeking certainty in appearances or conventional definitions of normality, the speaker imagines illuminating the hidden self. To bring light into the heart is to confront what is strange, wounded, or unknown within it and to recognize those qualities without rejection.

The conclusion therefore offers a cautious form of hope. Self-knowledge can transform estrangement into acceptance, while love can create connections where difference once produced distance. The true home of the soul is not necessarily a physical place or a fixed social identity, but an awakened heart capable of understanding itself and embracing others. By illuminating that inner space, the speaker suggests, even the grotesque and unfamiliar can become part of a larger, shared humanity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem that uses bizarre sideshow anomalies and natural oddities as metaphors for spiritual doubt, guilt, longing, and the search for an inner home.
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of town, where the salt flats rehearsed their white apocalypse, a carnival opened beneath a moon with two shadows.

Inside, the woman with a nest of moths beneath her tongue whispered prayers she could not release. Each time she tried, gray wings escaped between her teeth and battered themselves against the lanterns. I knew her as doubt: soft-bodied, powder-fingered, forever mistaking light for an answer.

Nearby, the man whose heart beat outside his chest kept it polished beneath a glass bell. He charged a coin to hear it confess. It said: I should have stayed. It said: I should have spoken. It said nothing that could be repaired. Around him, the audience cheered as if guilt were a marvelous animal, as if sorrow had been trained to bow.

Beyond the striped tents grew a forest of albino redwoods, their needles pale as unwritten letters. No bird nested there. The roots, unable to feed themselves, drank secretly from the darker trees. I walked among them longing to borrow a life from something certain. My hands became antlers. My name filled with snow.

At the final booth, a child displayed a staircase coiled inside a glass jar. “It goes down to the room you lost before you were born,” she said. I placed my ear against the glass and heard dishes being washed, a kettle beginning to sing, someone moving through the rooms without fear of departure.

I asked the child how to enter.

She pointed toward the desert, where stones were sailing slowly across the dry lake, leaving long tracks no one had witnessed them making. “Follow what moves when you are not looking.”

So I went out under the double-shadowed moon. Behind me, the carnival folded itself into a black flower. Ahead, the wandering stones dragged their invisible burdens across the earth.

All night I followed their scars.

By dawn, I understood nothing—but my antlers had caught a small, warm bird, and in the cup of its body, trembling above my brow, something like home began building itself from grass, from thread, from every question I had failed to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical monologue in which the speaker recalls a two-headed goat, a four-winged chicken, a seven-legged lamb, and other strange marvels before confessing that something grotesque is growing inside them.
counterfactuals.output:
I have seen wonders enough to ruin wonder.

Once, at the edge of a rain-black field, I saw a goat born with two heads—  
one crying toward the hills, the other toward the house,  
as if the little body could not decide  
which sorrow had called it into the world.  
Its four eyes shone like wet seeds.  
When one mouth slept, the other tasted the wind.

I saw a chicken with four wings  
beat itself pale against the dusk.  
It rose no higher than the fence,  
but oh, what thunder it made—  
a small storm stitched in feathers,  
dreaming twice as hard of heaven.

At the spring fair they showed us a seven-legged lamb  
laid gently in a box of straw.  
The farmer charged a penny to look.  
Children counted the hooves aloud, then counted again,  
because numbers become prayers  
when the body refuses arithmetic.

There were other marvels:  
a calf with a moon-white eye in its forehead,  
a piglet smooth as wax, without a mouth,  
an egg that held another egg,  
and inside that, a red bead trembling—  
life rehearsing itself in smaller and smaller rooms.

I remember them all.

I remember how we leaned close,  
how disgust and tenderness braided in our throats.  
We called them omens because we were afraid  
to call them kin.  
We whispered *monster*  
and meant: *the world has made something  
for which we have no cradle.*

Now, at night, I lie awake  
with both hands pressed beneath my ribs.

Something is growing there.

Not a child.  
Not anything blessed with a name.

It turns when the moon turns.  
It knocks softly against my bones.  
Sometimes I feel it unfolding—  
a wet wing, an extra jaw,  
a cluster of blind and listening eyes.  
Sometimes it seems to have many feet.  
Sometimes none.

And lately, when I speak,  
another voice moves under mine,  
testing my teeth.

So bring straw. Bring the little wooden box.  
Hang a curtain and charge a penny.  
Soon I too will be a marvel—  
the house with the wrong creature inside it,  
the single body crowded with impossible hungers.

Come close.

Count carefully.

I do not think it is finished with me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental paragraph inspired by old Ripley’s Believe It or Not! exhibits, blending precise names, places, and measurements with an intimate meditation on aging, love, and faith.
counterfactuals.output: In a glass case at the shuttered Orpheum Arcade in Muncie, Indiana, rests the wedding ring of Elias Voss—14-karat gold, 18.2 millimeters across—worn thin as onion skin after sixty-three years on the same finger; beside it, a card records that his wife, Miriam, grew exactly 4.7 centimeters shorter between 1951 and 2009, though Elias insisted she had only “moved closer to heaven.” There is also a human hair, 2.3 meters long, collected from Sister Agnes Bell at the Monastery of Saint Brigid, County Clare, and a stopped Elgin watch recovered from Lake Superior at a depth of 37.8 meters, its hands fixed at 6:14—the minute Samuel Orr learned to pray while drowning and, impossibly, did not drown. I study these measurements as if accuracy could keep loss from enlarging: your wrist narrowing beneath my thumb, my own face becoming my father’s by fractions, the bed remembering the weight of two bodies even when one rises first. Love, perhaps, is merely the most faithful instrument, registering what time removes; faith is what we call the trembling needle when no scale remains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly whimsical prose poem about a traveler burdened by emotional “chains” who wishes for a lighthouse lamp inside their skull to guide them home.
counterfactuals.output:
The traveler wore their sorrows like chains, though no blacksmith had forged them. Each link bore a small engraving: *almost*, *if only*, *too late*. They dragged behind through the dusk, chiming softly enough to be mistaken for sleigh bells by children and for teeth by wolves.

Home, meanwhile, had become a rumor told by chimneys.

So the traveler walked west, where the road narrowed into a ribbon, then a thread, then the long black hair of a drowned queen. Crows offered directions in exchange for memories. Mushrooms lit tiny green parlors beneath the trees. Even the moon, pale and officious, peered down as if checking a ledger.

“If only,” said the traveler, touching their brow, “there were a lighthouse lamp inside my skull.”

They imagined it there: a bright revolving eye behind the forehead, sweeping the inner sea. It would flash across drowned names, reefs of regret, the shipwrecked furniture of old rooms. It would warn every lost thing: *Here is the harbor. Here is the harbor. Here.*

But the skull remained a locked lantern, full of moths.

Still, near midnight, one small moth caught fire.

It fluttered behind the traveler’s eyes—not enough to banish the dark, not enough to melt the chains, but enough to make each link gleam. And in that poor, flickering radiance, the traveler saw that the chains did not stretch backward.

They stretched forward.

Toward a distant house with one window awake.

Toward a door already opening.

Toward home, which had been pulling all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a single dense, dreamlike passage that moves from cataloguing human, animal, and botanical curiosities to an invitation into the illuminated interior of the speaker’s heart.
counterfactuals.output: Come, count the curiosities gathered under my tongue: the sailor born with a blue crescent in his palm, the widow who hears snow rehearsing in the walls, the child whose shadow arrives an hour before him; the glass-winged moth, the fox asleep with one gold eye open, the pale eel knotting itself around a drowned bell; mandrake feet, orchid mouths, ferns unfurling their green alphabets, pears ripening with tiny storms at their cores, and a black rose drinking moonlight from a cracked porcelain cup—come past these cabinets of marvel and sorrow, past the antler, the feather, the seed in its velvet coffin, past all that crawls, blossoms, molts, and vanishes, and place your hand upon the small red door beneath my ribs: it is not locked; enter, and you will find my heart lit from within, every chamber burning softly, every wound a window, every beat calling you farther into the luminous house.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
